scenes.tts: Why would a glial cell wrap an axon in dozens of layers of membrane? And why are some axons never wrapped?
scenes.visual: Title card: Why Wrap, and How Much. A large wrapped axon beside a thin bare one, each with a question mark.
scenes.narration: Why would a glial cell wrap an axon in dozens of layers of membrane? And why are some axons never wrapped?

scenes.tts: Start with one patch of membrane. Current spreads to it from the active stretch behind. Before it can fire, that current must charge it.
scenes.visual: A short patch of axon membrane drawn as a capacitor; charge arrows fill it until a threshold line lights.
scenes.narration: Start with one patch of membrane. Current spreads to it from the active stretch behind. Before it can fire, that current must charge it.

scenes.tts: In a bare axon, current also leaks out at every point. So the signal is rebuilt on every patch. Less current is left to charge the patch ahead.
scenes.visual: A long bare axon; leak arrows fade outward along its length; the current arrow shrinks as it travels; a pulse is rebuilt patch by patch, slowly.
scenes.narration: In a bare axon, current also leaks out at every point. So the signal is rebuilt on every patch. Less current is left to charge the patch ahead.

scenes.tts: Myelin is glial membrane, wound many times around the axon and squeezed tight.
scenes.visual: Cross-section: a glial sheet spirals around the axon, then the turns squeeze together. Labels: oligodendrocyte, brain and spinal cord; Schwann cell, nerve.
scenes.narration: Myelin is glial membrane, wound many times around the axon and squeezed tight.

scenes.tts: Each turn adds two membranes in series. So the wall's capacitance falls. And its resistance rises. Far more of the current now reaches the next gap.
scenes.visual: Zoom on the sheath: membranes stacked in a row. A current arrow runs under the sheath to the next gap, thinner than at the start but much stronger than in the bare axon. On screen, small print: illustrative, 5 µm axon, g = 0.65, about 17 nm per turn, so about 80 turns and about 160 membranes.
scenes.narration: Each turn adds two membranes in series. So the wall's capacitance falls. And its resistance rises. Far more of the current now reaches the next gap.

scenes.tts: Those gaps are the nodes of Ron vee ay. The axon packs its sodium channels there.
scenes.visual: Axon with sheaths and short gaps labelled node of Ranvier; wrapped stretches labelled internode; sodium channels drawn as a dense cluster at each node, labelled high channel density.
scenes.caption: Those gaps are the nodes of Ranvier. The axon packs its sodium channels there.
scenes.narration: Those gaps are the nodes of Ranvier. The axon packs its sodium channels there.

scenes.tts: The signal is rebuilt at the nodes, so it seems to jump. This is saltatory conduction.
scenes.visual: A flash at one node, current under the sheath, a flash at the next node, and on along the axon. Label: saltatory conduction.
scenes.narration: The signal is rebuilt at the nodes, so it seems to jump. This is saltatory conduction.

scenes.tts: In a bare axon, speed rises with the square root of diameter. In a myelinated fiber, it rises in proportion to diameter.
scenes.visual: Plot of speed against diameter: a bending square-root curve labelled bare, a straight line labelled myelinated.
scenes.narration: In a bare axon, speed rises with the square root of diameter. In a myelinated fiber, it rises in proportion to diameter.

scenes.tts: So which axon gains more from a wrap, a thin one or a thick one?
scenes.visual: Two axons, 2 µm and 10 µm, each with a question mark and an empty gain box.
scenes.narration: So which axon gains more from a wrap, a thin one or a thick one?

scenes.tts: The thick one. In a simple model, the gain grows with the axon's size.
scenes.visual: Table builds: 2 µm axon, about 13 times; 5 µm, about 21 times; 10 µm, about 29 times. Small print: simple model, g = 0.65, bare speed √d m/s, myelinated 6 m/s per µm of fiber diameter. Footnote: Hursh's line is a rule for large fibers, so the small row is least reliable.
scenes.narration: The thick one. In a simple model, the gain grows with the axon's size.

scenes.tts: The axon diameter is the axon alone. The fiber diameter adds the myelin.
scenes.visual: Cross-section with two rulers: inner ruler on the axon, outer ruler across axon plus myelin. Example on screen: 6 µm axon, 10 µm fiber, g = 0.6.
scenes.narration: The axon diameter is the axon alone. The fiber diameter adds the myelin.

scenes.tts: Their ratio is the gee ratio. A thinner sheath on the same axon gives a higher gee ratio.
scenes.visual: On screen: g ratio = axon diameter ÷ fiber diameter. The sheath thins and the g readout rises.
scenes.caption: Their ratio is the g ratio. A thinner sheath on the same axon gives a higher g ratio.
scenes.narration: Their ratio is the g ratio. A thinner sheath on the same axon gives a higher g ratio.

scenes.tts: Healthy peripheral fibers sit near zero point six to zero point seven. That is close to the fastest value, but the optimum is broad.
scenes.visual: A flat-topped curve of relative speed against g ratio, labelled Rushton model, total fiber diameter held fixed; broad peak near 0.61; a wide shaded band from 0.6 to 0.7.
scenes.caption: Healthy peripheral fibers sit near 0.6 to 0.7. That is close to the fastest value, but the optimum is broad.
scenes.narration: Healthy peripheral fibers sit near 0.6 to 0.7. That is close to the fastest value, but the optimum is broad.

scenes.tts: Now the puzzle. In peripheral nerve, axons up to about one micrometer stay bare. Some cable models of small central fibers put the break-even for myelin much lower, so speed alone may not explain the cutoff.
scenes.visual: A Schwann cell holding several thin bare axons in grooves, beside a large wrapped axon. Label: up to about 1 µm, bare.
scenes.caption: Now the puzzle. In peripheral nerve, axons up to about 1 micrometer stay bare. Some cable models of small central fibers put the break-even for myelin much lower, so speed alone may not explain the cutoff.
scenes.narration: Now the puzzle. In peripheral nerve, axons up to about 1 micrometer stay bare. Some cable models of small central fibers put the break-even for myelin much lower, so speed alone may not explain the cutoff.

scenes.tts: Space and energy cost may matter too. Something in the tissue may decide.
scenes.visual: The speed plot fades; a question mark sits between the thin axons and the Schwann cell.
scenes.narration: Space and energy cost may matter too. Something in the tissue may decide.

scenes.tts: Here is the idea to carry. The speed gain is largest on large axons, and nerves do match the wrap to the axon. How?
scenes.visual: Guiding idea card, first line: match the wrap to the axon.
scenes.narration: Here is the idea to carry. The speed gain is largest on large axons, and nerves do match the wrap to the axon. How?

scenes.tts: In nerve, the axon decides. In the brain and spinal cord, the oligodendrocyte brings much of its own program.
scenes.visual: Guiding idea card completes: in nerve, the axon decides; in the brain and spinal cord, the oligodendrocyte brings much of its own program.
scenes.narration: In nerve, the axon decides. In the brain and spinal cord, the oligodendrocyte brings much of its own program.
